**The Quiet Rebellion of Ordinary Things**

There’s a kind of magic in the mundane, a quiet rebellion against the idea that life must be extraordinary to be meaningful. We are told, in subtle and not-so-subtle ways, that we must chase grand passions, achieve monumental success, or experience earth-shattering love to justify our existence. But what if the most radical act is simply to pay attention—to the way morning light slants through a window, to the sound of rain tapping against a roof, to the slow, steady rhythm of a breath in and out?

I’ve been thinking a lot about the small things lately. Not in the way of clichés—like "stop and smell the roses"—but in the way of resistance. The world is loud, insistent, demanding our attention in ways that leave us exhausted, fragmented. Algorithms decide what we see, capitalism tells us what we need, and social media flattens our emotions into performative squares of content. In this noise, the ordinary becomes a sanctuary, a place where we can reclaim our autonomy.

Take, for example, the act of making tea. It’s not just about boiling water and steeping leaves; it’s a ritual. The way the kettle hums as it heats, the way the steam curls into the air, the way the first sip burns just enough to remind you that you’re alive. There’s no productivity in it, no measurable outcome. And yet, in that moment, you are fully present. You are not scrolling, not multitasking, not optimizing. You are just… here. That, in itself, is a rebellion.

Or consider the way a book feels in your hands—the weight of it, the texture of the pages, the way the spine cracks when you open it for the first time. There’s something almost sacred in the act of reading, in the way words on a page can transport you to another time, another mind. In a world that prioritizes speed and efficiency, reading is slow. It demands patience. It asks you to sit still, to listen, to engage. That, too, is a rebellion.

I’ve been trying to notice these things more, not because I’m trying to be poetic or profound, but because I’m tired of living in a world that treats everything as a means to an end. We are so obsessed with outcomes—with likes, with promotions, with milestones—that we forget to live in the process. The journey is not just a path to the destination; it is the destination. The way the light changes in the afternoon, the way a friend’s laughter sounds over the phone, the way a cat stretches in a sunbeam—these are not distractions from life. They *are* life.

There’s a quote by the poet Mary Oliver that I keep coming back to: *"Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"* It’s a question that haunts me, not because I don’t have an answer, but because I’m afraid of the wrong kind of answer. I don’t want to say, *"I plan to work harder, to achieve more, to be more."* I want to say, *"I plan to notice. I plan to be present. I plan to love the ordinary as fiercely as I love the extraordinary."*

Because here’s the thing: the extraordinary is just the ordinary with a spotlight on it. A sunset is just the sky doing what it always does, but we call it beautiful because we’ve stopped to look. A deep conversation with a friend is just two people talking, but we call it meaningful because we’ve chosen to listen. The magic isn’t in the thing itself; it’s in the attention we give it.

I’ve been thinking about this a lot in the context of creativity. We live in a culture that glorifies the "genius," the person who creates something groundbreaking, something that changes the world. But what about the person who writes a poem no one will ever read? What about the person who paints a picture just because it brings them joy? What about the person who gardens not to grow food, but to watch something grow? Is that any less valid? I don’t think so. In fact, I think it might be more radical. It’s a refusal to measure art—or life—by its impact. It’s a declaration that creation is not just for the world, but for the self.

There’s a story I love about the artist Agnes Martin. She was known for her minimalist paintings—subtle grids and lines that seemed almost invisible at first glance. Once, a visitor to her studio asked her why she painted such quiet, unassuming work. She replied, *"I paint with my back to the world."* It wasn’t about fame or recognition; it was about the act itself. That, to me, is the ultimate rebellion—not to seek approval, but to create for the sake of creation.

I’ve been trying to apply this to my own life. Not in a grand, sweeping way, but in small, daily choices. To write even when no one is reading. To cook a meal just because I enjoy the process. To take a walk without a destination. To sit in silence instead of filling the space with noise. These are not grand gestures, but they are acts of defiance. They are a way of saying, *"I refuse to let my life be dictated by what is productive, what is marketable, what is impressive. I will live for the sake of living."*

There’s a danger in romanticizing the ordinary, of course. Not everyone has the luxury of slowing down. For some, the mundane is not a sanctuary but a struggle—bills to pay, children to feed, jobs that drain rather than fulfill. I don’t mean to suggest that everyone should just "stop and smell the roses" as if that’s a solution to systemic problems. But I do think there’s value in reclaiming the small, quiet moments where we can. In a world that demands so much of us, those moments can be a form of resistance.

I’ve been thinking about this in the context of grief, too. When someone we love dies, the world doesn’t stop. The sun still rises, the dishes still need to be washed, the emails still need to be answered. It feels wrong, almost obscene, that life should continue when something so monumental has happened. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe the ordinary is what carries us through the extraordinary pain. Maybe the fact that the world keeps going is not a betrayal, but a reminder that life is bigger than our individual sorrows.

There’s a line in a poem by Naomi Shihab Nye that says, *"Before you know kindness as the deepest thing inside, / you must know sorrow as the other deepest thing."* I think the same is true of joy. Before you can know joy as the deepest thing inside, you must know the ordinary as the other deepest thing. Because joy is not just in the big moments—the weddings, the promotions, the once-in-a-lifetime trips. It’s in the small, quiet things, too. The way a child’s hand feels in yours. The way a favorite song sounds when you hear it unexpectedly. The way a cup of coffee tastes on a cold morning.

I don’t know if any of this makes sense. Maybe I’m just trying to justify my own love of the mundane. But I think there’s something powerful in it. In a world that is constantly telling us to be more, do more, want more, the act of choosing to be content with less—with the quiet, the slow, the unremarkable—feels like a kind of freedom.

So I’ll keep making tea. I’ll keep reading books. I’ll keep writing even when no one is reading. I’ll keep noticing the way the light falls, the way the rain sounds, the way a breath feels. And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough. Maybe that’s the whole point.
